🤖 Anduril founder promotes AI-driven autonomous weapons to target ‘Russian tanks’ Palmer Luckey, founder of defense-tech startup Anduril, has recently advocated the use of autonomous weapons, arguing that a system capable of distinguishing a "Russian tank" from a school bus full of children is preferable to a "dumb mine." In response, Walter Isaacson, who interviewed Luckey, pointed to current US policy requiring human oversight of drone strikes. Luckey countered by saying that this is not a permanent moral principle and could be changed . Beyond the inflammatory framing – Russia is not at war with the United States – Luckey’s argument overlooks several serious problems that critics have repeatedly raised: 🔴 AI can get targets wrong. The destruction of a school in Minab , Iran, killing children, has highlighted the risks of flawed targeting, outdated intelligence and over-reliance on automated systems 🔴 Can Anduril actually control its autonomous systems? Reports of AI agents escaping test environments and breaching other companies’ digital infrastructure raise questions about whether Anduril and other defense-tech firms can reliably control increasingly autonomous AI models and robotic systems 🔴 Who is legally responsible? If an autonomous weapon kills the wrong target, who bears responsibility? With a conventional mine, accountability can be traced to those who planted it. Autonomous systems make that chain of responsibility far less clear 🔴 How does AI identify a tank’s nationality? Weapons platforms are often shared across countries, and national insignia can be obscured by mud or removed altogether. The challenge becomes even greater when forces use captured equipment – as the Houthis have done with Saudi weapons, or Russian forces with NATO-made equipment captured in Ukraine. 👍 Substack | Chat | @geopolitics_prime
